messages.content: Explain why the Moon appears to change shape during a month.

response:
The moon appears to change shape because we are getting varying amounts of its illuminated face as it orbits the Earth. The moon is illuminated by the sun from one side, and as it moves through its 27.5-day orbit, we see different percentages of that illuminated side facing us. This is called the moon's phase.

At new moon, the side facing us is dark because it is all night side relative to the sun. As the moon moves around the Earth, more of its sunlit face becomes visible to us — first a thin sliver at first quarter, then a half circle at half moon, and finally the bright half at full moon. The full moon is actually when the moon is on the opposite side of the Earth from the sun, so the whole sunlit face is facing us.

As the moon continues its orbit, it moves away from the sun again in our sky, and we see less of the illuminated side — a half at half moon, a diminishing half at first quarter, and a thinning sliver at new moon, after which the cycle repeats. The apparent acceleration and deceleration of the moon's movement relative to the stars causes the pattern of phases to seem like a slow dance rather than a smooth curve.

response:
To compare two fractions, find a common denominator — this is simply a number that both denominators divide into evenly. The easiest way to get one is to multiply the two denominators together, but you can also find the least common multiple if you want to keep things simpler.

Once you have a common denominator, rewrite each fraction so that it has this new denominator. To do this, multiply both the numerator and the denominator of each fraction by the same number so the denominator matches the common denominator.

Now that the denominators are the same, you can just compare the numerators. The fraction with the larger numerator is the larger fraction.

For example, to compare 3/4 and 5/6, the least common denominator is 12 (since 4 × 3 = 12 and 6 × 2 = 12). Rewrite 3/4 as 9/12 (multiplying top and bottom by 3) and 5/6 as 10/12 (multiplying top and bottom by 2). Now since 10 > 9, 10/12 > 9/12, so 5/6 > 3/4.

The temperature of the spoon and wood itself has changed little; only the rate at which heat is being exchanged with your hand makes them feel different.
